To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
shorter antibiotic regimens are as effective as longer ones and that they exert less selective pressure, thus preventing the emergence of resistance.
shorter courses of antibiotics exert less selective pressure than longer treatments.
the prescription of antibiotics should be limited, with shorter treatment duration and the use of biomarkers to guide treatment.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new strategies for the rational use of antibiotics in the treatment of common infections.
understanding the mechanisms that lead to the emergence of resistance, as well as the factors that contribute to the spread of resistance genes.
the development of new strategies to delay the emergence and dissemination, or to prevent the development, of antibiotic resistance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
shorter antibiotic treatments are as effective as long-term treatments in most infections, with the exception of some specific cases.
the prescription of antibiotics should be limited to those cases where it is really necessary, and that treatment duration should be as short as possible.
antibiotic stewardship programmes are essential to reduce antibiotic resistance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of shorter antibiotic treatments should be encouraged in order to reduce antibiotic resistance.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the prescription of shorter treatments can be an effective tool in the fight against antimicrobial resistance.
the use of shorter antibiotic regimens is an essential step towards delaying the emergence and dissemination resistance.
, in addition to the prescription of fewer and narrower-spectrum antibiotics, the duration of antibiotic treatment should also be reduced to delay resistance.
